questions.q: Which statement best defines forecasting in a business context?
options: Setting the sales figure that management wants the team to achieve next year, based on its growth ambitions
Predicting future values as accurately as possible using historical data and knowledge of likely future events
Recording and reporting last year's sales figures accurately so that the past performance is well understood
Guaranteeing what will happen in the future
questions.answer: Predicting future values as accurately as possible using historical data and knowledge of likely future events
questions.explanation: Forecasting estimates what is likely to happen using data and judgement. Confusing it with target-setting is the most common mistake, because a target is what management wants, not what is likely.

questions.q: How does a forecast differ from a goal (target)?
options: A forecast is what is likely to happen; a goal is what management would like to happen
A forecast is always set higher than a goal so that the sales team stays motivated
A goal is based on data, while a forecast is based only on opinion
There is no difference; both words describe the same number
questions.answer: A forecast is what is likely to happen; a goal is what management would like to happen
questions.explanation: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos stress that forecasts, goals and plans are different. Treating them as the same leads to forecasts inflated to match ambitions.

questions.q: Which statement about forecasts is generally true?
options: A good forecast should always equal the actual value exactly, otherwise the model is wrong
Forecasts are only needed when the future is certain
Forecast errors prove that forecasting has no business value
Forecasts are rarely exactly right, so an estimate of the likely error is useful
questions.answer: Forecasts are rarely exactly right, so an estimate of the likely error is useful
questions.explanation: Because the future is uncertain, forecasts carry error; good practice reports a range or error measure. Expecting perfect accuracy is a misconception.

questions.q: According to Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, which factor makes an event MORE predictable?
options: The forecast itself changes how people involved behave
Very little historical data is available
We understand well the factors that drive it
The environment changes rapidly with no stable pattern
questions.answer: We understand well the factors that drive it
questions.explanation: Predictability improves with good understanding of drivers, plenty of data and forecasts that do not affect the outcome. The other options all reduce predictability.

questions.q: Qualitative (judgemental) forecasting methods are most appropriate when:
options: Several years of clean monthly sales data are available for the product in question
Little or no relevant historical data is available, as for a new product
The company wants a purely automatic forecast with no human input
The variable follows a very stable seasonal pattern
questions.answer: Little or no relevant historical data is available, as for a new product
questions.explanation: Judgemental methods are used when data are absent or not relevant. With plenty of stable history, quantitative methods are usually preferred.

questions.q: Quantitative forecasting methods require two conditions. Which pair is correct?
options: Numerical data about the past exist, and some past patterns can be assumed to continue
Expert opinion is available from senior managers, and the future is known to be certain
A large marketing budget exists, and competitors share their data
Management has set a target, and the data are in percentages
questions.answer: Numerical data about the past exist, and some past patterns can be assumed to continue
questions.explanation: Quantitative forecasting rests on past numeric data and the continuity assumption. Expert opinion belongs to qualitative forecasting.

questions.q: A manufacturer decides how many units to produce next month. Which function is using forecasts here?
options: Statutory audit of last year's accounts
Legal and regulatory compliance
Investor relations reporting
Operations / production planning
questions.answer: Operations / production planning
questions.explanation: Production scheduling depends on a demand forecast. The other functions mainly report on the past or on regulations rather than planning output.

questions.q: A time series forecasting model predicts a variable using:
options: Only the opinions and experience of senior managers
Other explanatory variables such as price and advertising, but not its own past values
Past values of the same variable recorded over time
Random numbers generated by a computer
questions.answer: Past values of the same variable recorded over time
questions.explanation: Time series models extrapolate patterns in the variable's own history. Using other drivers describes an explanatory (causal) model.

questions.q: A model that predicts sales from price, advertising spend and competitor activity is called:
options: A naive model
An explanatory (causal) model
A qualitative judgemental model
A pure time series model
questions.answer: An explanatory (causal) model
questions.explanation: Explanatory models relate the forecast variable to its drivers. A pure time series model uses only the variable's own past.

questions.q: In forecasting, the term 'forecast horizon' refers to:
options: How far into the future the forecast is made
The number of years of historical data used to fit the model
The accuracy level of the forecast
The geographical area the forecast covers
questions.answer: How far into the future the forecast is made
questions.explanation: The horizon is the lead time between now and the period being forecast. It is often confused with the length of the history used.

questions.q: A Bengaluru bakery chain bakes each day's bread based on a next-day demand forecast. What is the main business benefit of a good forecast here?
options: Higher prices for every product because customers expect freshness
Complete elimination of day-to-day demand uncertainty
No further need to record daily sales in the stores
Less wastage of unsold bread and fewer stock-outs
questions.answer: Less wastage of unsold bread and fewer stock-outs
questions.explanation: For perishables, forecasts balance waste against lost sales. No forecast eliminates uncertainty, so claiming that is the main error.

questions.q: Why is next week's INR/USD exchange rate much harder to forecast than tomorrow's electricity demand in Mumbai?
options: Exchange rates have no historical data available, while electricity demand has decades of recorded history
Electricity demand has no seasonal pattern, so it is simple to extrapolate from yesterday's value
Traders act on exchange-rate forecasts, so forecasts affect the outcome; electricity demand drivers are well understood
Exchange rates are fixed once a year by the government
questions.answer: Traders act on exchange-rate forecasts, so forecasts affect the outcome; electricity demand drivers are well understood
questions.explanation: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos contrast these two cases: exchange rates are hard because forecasts feed back into trading, whereas electricity demand has well-understood drivers and long history.

questions.q: A start-up is launching a new plant-based milk brand in India with no sales history. Which forecasting approach is most suitable at launch?
options: A seasonal time series model fitted to the brand's own past monthly sales
Expert opinion, market surveys and analogy with similar launches
A naive forecast equal to last month's sales of the brand
Wait until three years of data exist before forecasting anything
questions.answer: Expert opinion, market surveys and analogy with similar launches
questions.explanation: Without history, time series models cannot be fitted, so judgement and analogies are used. Waiting is not an option because launch decisions need numbers now.

questions.q: A sales head says: 'Our forecast for next year is Rs 12 crore because that is our target.' What is the main problem with this statement?
options: It confuses a target with a forecast, which should be an unbiased estimate of what is likely
Forecasts should always be stated in units of product, never in rupees, so the figure is invalid
Targets should always be set lower than forecasts so that teams can beat them
There is no problem; forecasts and targets should be identical
questions.answer: It confuses a target with a forecast, which should be an unbiased estimate of what is likely
questions.explanation: Plans built on a target dressed up as a forecast lead to over-stocking and over-hiring if the target is missed. Keep the forecast honest and treat any gap as a planning issue.

questions.q: A forecast states: next month's demand is 1,000 units, with an 80% prediction interval of 850 to 1,150 units. What does this mean?
options: Demand will be exactly 1,000 units, and the interval only shows rounding
Demand will be at least 80% of 1,000 units, that is 800 units or more
Demand is certain to lie between 850 and 1,150 units next month
There is about an 80% chance actual demand falls between 850 and 1,150 units
questions.answer: There is about an 80% chance actual demand falls between 850 and 1,150 units
questions.explanation: A prediction interval expresses uncertainty with a stated probability. Reading it as certainty, or reading the point forecast as exact, are the common errors.

questions.q: Which situation is best suited to a time series forecasting approach?
options: Forecasting sales of a product category that does not yet exist in India
Estimating how a 10% price cut will change demand for a detergent
Forecasting daily ATM cash withdrawals using three years of daily history
Assessing the demand effect of a new competitor entering the market
questions.answer: Forecasting daily ATM cash withdrawals using three years of daily history
questions.explanation: Long, regular history of the same variable suits time series methods. The price-cut and competitor questions need explanatory (what-if) models or judgement.

questions.q: A firm predicts air-conditioner sales using forecasted temperature for the coming month. This approach is:
options: A pure time series model, because temperature is itself recorded over time
An explanatory model, because sales are linked to an external driver
A qualitative method, because weather forecasts involve human judgement
A naive method, because it ignores past sales
questions.answer: An explanatory model, because sales are linked to an external driver
questions.explanation: Using an external predictor (temperature) makes it explanatory. The fact that the predictor varies over time does not make it a pure time series model.

questions.q: A news report forecasts that a cooperative bank may fail, and depositors rush to withdraw money, causing the failure. This illustrates:
options: A forecast influencing the very outcome it predicts
A purely seasonal pattern in bank withdrawals
A random error with no identifiable cause behind it
A highly predictable event with stable, well-understood drivers
questions.answer: A forecast influencing the very outcome it predicts
questions.explanation: When forecasts change behaviour, the event becomes harder to predict, one of the predictability factors in Hyndman & Athanasopoulos.

questions.q: Why do firms continue to forecast even though forecasts are never perfectly accurate?
options: Because regulators require every company's sales forecast to be exactly correct each quarter
Because forecasting removes the need for planning and budgeting altogether
Because inaccurate forecasts are always cheaper to produce than accurate ones
Capacity, stock and staffing decisions must be made before demand is known, and a reasoned estimate beats guessing
questions.answer: Capacity, stock and staffing decisions must be made before demand is known, and a reasoned estimate beats guessing
questions.explanation: Forecasting is valuable because lead times force early decisions. Its value lies in reducing, not eliminating, uncertainty.

questions.q: A retail chain estimates that Diwali demand will rise 20%, then decides to hire 50 temporary staff. Which part is the forecast?
options: Deciding to hire 50 temporary staff for the season
Approving the budget for the temporary staff
Estimating the 20% rise in Diwali demand
Training the new staff before Diwali
questions.answer: Estimating the 20% rise in Diwali demand
questions.explanation: The forecast is the estimate of what will happen; hiring is the plan made in response. Students often label the decision itself as the forecast.

questions.q: A dairy sells fresh milk with a one-day shelf life. An unsold litre costs Rs 20 (wasted), while a litre of unmet demand loses Rs 5 margin. The demand forecast is symmetric around 10,000 litres. What production decision is most sensible?
options: Produce exactly 10,000 litres, because the decision should always equal the central forecast
Produce below 10,000 litres, near the 20th percentile of demand, since excess costs more than shortage
Produce above 10,000 litres, near the 80th percentile of demand, to avoid losing any customers
Produce 20,000 litres so that any possible demand can be covered
questions.answer: Produce below 10,000 litres, near the 20th percentile of demand, since excess costs more than shortage
questions.explanation: The critical ratio is shortage cost / (shortage + excess cost) = 5/(5+20) = 0.20, so the best quantity is the 20th percentile. The 80th-percentile distractor flips the ratio (20/25).

questions.q: An e-commerce firm has only 3 months of sales for a new 'smart home' category, but 5 years of data for a similar earlier category ('wearables'). What is the best forecasting approach?
options: Use the wearables launch curve as an analogy, adjust it with expert judgement, and update as data arrive
Fit a complex seasonal model to the 3 months of smart home data alone, since recent data matter most
Ignore all data and use the category manager's sales target
Copy the wearables sales numbers exactly, without adjustment
questions.answer: Use the wearables launch curve as an analogy, adjust it with expert judgement, and update as data arrive
questions.explanation: With short history, analogy plus judgement is the most defensible approach and it improves as data accumulate. Fitting seasonality to 3 months is impossible, and copying the analogue blindly ignores real differences.

questions.q: A retailer's forecasting model, built on five stable years of data, failed badly during the 2020 lockdown. Which assumption of quantitative forecasting was violated?
options: That forecasts must always be expressed in percentage terms
That management judgement should never be used in forecasting
That the sales data contained no seasonal pattern
That past patterns would continue into the future
questions.answer: That past patterns would continue into the future
questions.explanation: Quantitative methods assume continuity of past patterns. A structural shock breaks that assumption, which is when judgement and scenarios become essential.

questions.q: Using the predictability factors in Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, which of these is MOST predictable?
options: The INR/USD exchange rate six months from now
The Sensex closing level on a particular date next year
Peak electricity demand in a city tomorrow afternoon
Sales of an entirely new product category three years from now
questions.answer: Peak electricity demand in a city tomorrow afternoon
questions.explanation: Electricity demand has well-understood drivers, long history and is not affected by the forecast. Financial prices react to forecasts, and new categories lack data.

questions.q: A manager argues: 'Our forecasts are often wrong, so let us stop forecasting and just react to demand.' What is the best response?
options: Agree, because reacting to demand after it occurs is always cheaper than planning ahead of it
Every plan already assumes some future demand, so make it explicit, measure its error and set buffers
Agree, but only for products whose demand shows strong seasonal patterns
Disagree, because a better model will eventually make forecasts perfectly accurate
questions.answer: Every plan already assumes some future demand, so make it explicit, measure its error and set buffers
questions.explanation: Lead times mean decisions are made before demand is known, so an implicit forecast exists anyway. Promising perfect accuracy is the opposite mistake.

questions.q: The statistical forecast shows 8% sales growth next year, but the board's target is 15%. What should management do?
options: Plan operations on the 8% forecast and close the 7-point gap with specific initiatives
Raise the forecast to 15% so that production, inventory and hiring plans all match the board's target
Lower the target to 8%, because a target must always equal the forecast
Average the two figures and plan all operations for 11.5% growth
questions.answer: Plan operations on the 8% forecast and close the 7-point gap with specific initiatives
questions.explanation: Forecasts should stay unbiased; the gap between forecast and target is what plans and initiatives must address. Inflating the forecast to the target leads to excess inventory and costs if the target is missed.

questions.q: A 200-room Goa hotel forecasts 160 rooms sold for a December weekend (80% interval 130 to 195). A tour operator wants 30 rooms at a deep discount. What is the best assessment?
options: Accept without further thought, because 160 + 30 = 190 rooms is below the 200-room capacity
Reject outright, because the point forecast alone already exceeds the hotel's capacity
The interval is irrelevant here; only the point forecast should guide the decision
It fits the point forecast (190 rooms), but the interval shows a real risk of displacing full-rate guests
questions.answer: It fits the point forecast (190 rooms), but the interval shows a real risk of displacing full-rate guests
questions.explanation: If demand is near the upper end (195), adding 30 rooms would need 225 rooms, displacing full-rate guests. Ignoring the interval is the common mistake.

questions.q: A firm builds an explanatory model: ice-cream sales = f(temperature). What is a key practical limitation when using it to forecast next month's sales?
options: Explanatory models cannot use numerical data such as temperature readings
Temperature has no relationship with ice-cream sales in Indian cities
Next month's temperature must itself be forecast, adding its uncertainty
The model can only reproduce past periods, never future ones
questions.answer: Next month's temperature must itself be forecast, adding its uncertainty
questions.explanation: Explanatory models need future values of the predictors, which are often uncertain. This is why time series models are sometimes preferred for short-term forecasts.

questions.q: A company sells 2,000 SKUs. A low-value, stable SKU (Rs 50,000 annual sales) is forecast with a simple method. An analyst proposes a complex machine-learning model costing much more effort for this SKU. What is the best judgement?
options: Always use the most complex model available for every SKU, since accuracy matters equally everywhere
Match effort to decision value: keep the simple method here and focus complex work on high-value items
Stop forecasting low-value SKUs entirely and reorder them at random intervals
Adopt the complex model, because added complexity always improves accuracy
questions.answer: Match effort to decision value: keep the simple method here and focus complex work on high-value items
questions.explanation: Forecasting has a cost, and its benefit depends on the decision it supports. Complexity does not guarantee accuracy, especially for stable series.

questions.q: Which statement about the nature of a good forecasting model is most accurate?
options: It captures genuine patterns in the data without replicating one-off past events
It fits every past data point exactly, because a perfect historical fit guarantees good forecasts
It is always the most mathematically complex model available to the analyst
Its accuracy stays the same no matter how far ahead it forecasts
questions.answer: It captures genuine patterns in the data without replicating one-off past events
questions.explanation: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos note good models capture real patterns but do not replicate one-off events. Perfect fit to history usually signals overfitting, and accuracy falls as the horizon grows.

references: Forecasting means estimating what is likely to happen in the future, such as next month's sales or next year's cash needs, using past data and knowledge about upcoming events. It is different from a target, which is what we want to happen, and from a plan, which is how we respond. Forecasts are never perfectly accurate, so a good forecast also tells us the likely range of error. Forecasting matters because most business decisions, like buying stock, hiring staff or building capacity, must be made before demand is known. Some things are easier to predict than others: we can forecast well when we understand the drivers, have enough data, and the forecast itself does not change the outcome.

Think of a supermarket chain like DMart planning for Diwali. It must order stock, schedule staff and arrange trucks weeks before customers arrive. A forecast gives the best estimate of demand, for example 25% higher than normal, based on past Diwali sales and this year's promotions. If they do not forecast, they will either run out of popular items or be stuck with unsold stock. The forecast will not be exact, so they also plan a buffer. When there is no history, like a new product, they use judgement, surveys and similar products. When there is plenty of data, they use quantitative methods such as time series or causal models.

As a manager, every decision involving the future already contains a forecast, whether stated or not. Forecasting makes that assumption explicit so we can plan inventory, production, staffing, budgets and capacity sensibly. A good forecast is an honest, unbiased estimate of what is likely, not the target we wish for, and it comes with a sense of uncertainty, such as a range. Forecasts can be qualitative, using expert judgement when data are scarce, or quantitative, using historical data and assuming past patterns continue. Their usefulness depends on predictability: well-understood drivers and good data help. Since errors are inevitable, we should measure accuracy and keep buffers rather than abandon forecasting.

topics.topic: Components, Types of Forecasts: Short-term, Medium-term, Long-term

questions.q: Short-term forecasts typically cover a period of:
options: 3 months to 3 years
3 to 10 years
Days to a few months (usually up to about 3 months)
More than 10 years
questions.answer: Days to a few months (usually up to about 3 months)
questions.explanation: Short-range forecasts usually run up to about 3 months (at most a year) and support scheduling and replenishment. 3 months to 3 years is the medium-term range.

questions.q: Medium-term forecasts typically cover a period of about:
options: One day to one week
3 months to 3 years
Up to 3 months only
10 years or more
questions.answer: 3 months to 3 years
questions.explanation: Medium-range forecasts span roughly 3 months to 3 years and support aggregate planning and budgeting. Up to 3 months is short term.

questions.q: Long-term forecasts (usually 3 years or more) are mainly used for:
options: Capacity expansion, facility location and new product or market strategy
Daily delivery route planning
Weekly shift rosters
Hourly call-centre staffing
questions.answer: Capacity expansion, facility location and new product or market strategy
questions.explanation: Long-range forecasts guide strategic decisions that take years to implement. Routing and rosters are short-term operational decisions.

questions.q: Which decision relies mainly on a short-term forecast?
options: Building a new manufacturing plant
Entering a new country market
Deciding the next five-year capital budget
Scheduling store staff for next week
questions.answer: Scheduling store staff for next week
questions.explanation: Weekly staffing uses near-term demand. Plants, market entry and five-year budgets are long-term strategic decisions.

questions.q: Which decision relies mainly on a long-term forecast?
options: Placing tomorrow's vegetable order for a busy Koramangala restaurant
Allocating trucks for this week's deliveries
Deciding whether to set up a new manufacturing plant in Gujarat
Planning next month's overtime
questions.answer: Deciding whether to set up a new manufacturing plant in Gujarat
questions.explanation: A new plant takes years to build and pay back, so it needs a long-range forecast. The others are short-term operational choices.

questions.q: The trend component of a time series is:
options: A pattern that repeats every year at the same time
The long-run upward or downward movement in the data
Unpredictable one-off fluctuations
Rises and falls of irregular length linked to the economy
questions.answer: The long-run upward or downward movement in the data
questions.explanation: Trend is the long-term direction. A pattern repeating at fixed intervals is seasonality.

questions.q: Seasonality in a time series refers to:
options: A regular pattern that repeats over a fixed, known period such as a year or a week
A long-run steady increase
Fluctuations of varying length tied to business cycles
Random noise that cannot be explained
questions.answer: A regular pattern that repeats over a fixed, known period such as a year or a week
questions.explanation: Seasonality has a fixed period (e.g., festive peaks every October-November). Fluctuations of varying length are cyclical, not seasonal.

questions.q: The cyclical component of a time series refers to:
options: Patterns that repeat every week
The long-run average growth rate
Errors made by the forecaster
Rises and falls that are not of fixed period, often linked to economic or business cycles lasting more than a year
questions.answer: Rises and falls that are not of fixed period, often linked to economic or business cycles lasting more than a year
questions.explanation: Cycles have variable length and are usually tied to the economy. Fixed-period patterns are seasonal.

questions.q: The irregular (random) component of a time series is:
options: The steady growth in sales over years
A festive peak that occurs every year
Unpredictable fluctuations left after removing trend, seasonal and cyclical effects
The forecast made by the manager
questions.answer: Unpredictable fluctuations left after removing trend, seasonal and cyclical effects
questions.explanation: The irregular component is the residual noise. It cannot be forecast, unlike trend and seasonality.

questions.q: A forecast of how quickly electric-vehicle battery costs will fall over the next decade is an example of:
options: A demand forecast for next week
A technological forecast
A short-term sales forecast
An inventory reorder forecast
questions.answer: A technological forecast
questions.explanation: Forecasts are also classified by subject: economic, technological and demand forecasts. Predicting the pace of technical change is technological forecasting.

questions.q: Ice-cream sales in Chennai peak every April-May and dip every December-January. This pattern is best described as:
options: Seasonal
Cyclical
Trend
Irregular
questions.answer: Seasonal
questions.explanation: The pattern repeats at the same time every year, so it is seasonal. Cyclical movements do not have a fixed period.

questions.q: Passenger car sales in India fell during an economic slowdown and recovered over the following years as the economy improved, with no fixed timing. This movement is best described as:
options: Seasonal
Irregular
Trend
Cyclical
questions.answer: Cyclical
questions.explanation: Multi-year rises and falls linked to the economy, without a fixed period, are cyclical. Seasonality repeats at a fixed calendar interval.

questions.q: A store's sales drop sharply on one day because of a local bandh, then return to normal. This is an example of:
options: The trend component
The seasonal component
The irregular (random) component
The cyclical component
questions.answer: The irregular (random) component
questions.explanation: A one-off unpredictable event shows up as irregular variation. It does not repeat at fixed intervals and is not long-run.

questions.q: UPI transaction volumes in India have risen steadily year after year since 2017. This is primarily:
options: Seasonality
A trend
An irregular component
A cyclical component
questions.answer: A trend
questions.explanation: A sustained long-run increase is a trend. Month-to-month festive bumps on top of it would be seasonality.

questions.q: Generally, which forecasts tend to be more accurate, and why?
options: Short-term forecasts, because there is less time for conditions and patterns to change
Long-term forecasts, because they use more years of data
Long-term forecasts, because random short-term errors cancel each other out over many years
All horizons are equally accurate if the same model is used
questions.answer: Short-term forecasts, because there is less time for conditions and patterns to change
questions.explanation: Uncertainty grows with the horizon, so short-term forecasts are usually more accurate. More historical data does not offset the growing uncertainty of the far future.

questions.q: An FMCG company sets workforce levels and monthly production rates for the next 6 to 12 months (aggregate planning). Which forecast type does it mainly need?
options: Short-term forecast
Long-term forecast
Technological forecast
Medium-term forecast
questions.answer: Medium-term forecast
questions.explanation: Aggregate planning over 6-12 months uses medium-range forecasts. Short-term forecasts are for days/weeks; long-term for strategic capacity.

questions.q: Long-term forecasts are usually prepared at what level of detail?
options: Individual SKU and store level by day, as long-term plans need the most detail
Hourly level for each employee
Aggregate level, such as total sales or product families
Single-transaction level
questions.answer: Aggregate level, such as total sales or product families
questions.explanation: Long-range decisions (capacity, strategy) need aggregate numbers, and aggregates are also more predictable far ahead. SKU-day detail suits short-term forecasts.

questions.q: In a multiplicative model Y = T x S x I, the trend value for December is 1,000 units, the December seasonal index is 1.25 and the irregular factor is 1. What is the expected December value?
options: 1,250 units
800 units
1,025 units
questions.answer: 1,250 units
questions.explanation: 1,000 x 1.25 x 1 = 1,250. Adding the index (1,001.25) treats a multiplicative index as additive; dividing (800) is the deseasonalising step, not forecasting.

questions.q: In an additive model Y = T + S + I, the trend value is 500, the seasonal effect is +60 and the irregular effect is -10. What is Y?
questions.explanation: 500 + 60 - 10 = 550. 570 ignores the minus sign on the irregular term and 560 drops the irregular term entirely.

questions.q: A company wants to forecast the size of India's market for drone deliveries 10 years from now. Which method is most typical?
options: A 3-month moving average of the last quarter's drone delivery sales figures
Simple exponential smoothing on weekly data
A naive forecast equal to this month's value
Judgemental methods such as Delphi panels and scenario analysis
questions.answer: Judgemental methods such as Delphi panels and scenario analysis
questions.explanation: Long-term forecasts of emerging markets have little relevant data, so expert and scenario methods dominate. Smoothing methods suit short-term forecasting of stable series.

questions.q: A hotel's Q3 revenue was Rs 150 lakh and the Q3 seasonal index is 1.20. What is the deseasonalised Q3 revenue?
options: Rs 180 lakh
Rs 148.8 lakh
Rs 125 lakh
Rs 30 lakh
questions.answer: Rs 125 lakh
questions.explanation: Deseasonalise by dividing: 150 / 1.20 = 125. Multiplying (180) applies the seasonal effect twice instead of removing it.

questions.q: A clothing retailer's festive peaks grow larger every year as overall sales grow (e.g., peak +20 lakh when base was 100, +40 lakh when base was 200). Which decomposition is more appropriate and why?
options: Additive, because the seasonal swing stays constant in absolute terms
Multiplicative, because the size of the seasonal swing is proportional to the level of the series
Additive, because sales are measured in rupees
Neither; seasonality cannot coexist with a trend
questions.answer: Multiplicative, because the size of the seasonal swing is proportional to the level of the series
questions.explanation: When seasonal swings scale with the level (here 20% each time), a multiplicative model fits. An additive model assumes a constant absolute swing, which is not the case here.

questions.q: A cement company sees demand upswings lasting 3 to 5 years, of varying length, tied to construction booms. Why is this not seasonality, and what is the managerial implication?
options: Its period is not fixed, so it is cyclical; its timing is hard to predict and should be handled with economic indicators and scenarios
It is seasonal because it repeats; a seasonal index will forecast it precisely
It is a trend because it lasts more than a year; extrapolate it linearly
It is irregular noise and should be ignored in planning
questions.answer: Its period is not fixed, so it is cyclical; its timing is hard to predict and should be handled with economic indicators and scenarios
questions.explanation: Cycles vary in length, so seasonal indices cannot capture them and linear extrapolation misreads turning points. Leading indicators and scenarios are the usual approach.

questions.q: An FMCG firm makes three decisions: (a) daily truck dispatch to distributors, (b) next year's quarterly volumes at contract manufacturers, (c) entering two new states in five years. Which mapping of forecast horizons is correct?
options: (a) medium-term, (b) short-term, (c) long-term
(a) short-term, (b) long-term, (c) medium-term
(a) long-term, (b) medium-term, (c) short-term
(a) short-term, (b) medium-term, (c) long-term
questions.answer: (a) short-term, (b) medium-term, (c) long-term
questions.explanation: Daily dispatch is short-term, a one-year contract-manufacturing plan is medium-term and five-year market entry is long-term. Confusing (b) with long-term is common because it involves annual numbers.

questions.q: A firm's one-month-ahead forecasts have about 5% error, but its three-year forecasts were off by 35%. How should management use long-term forecasts?
options: Stop using long-term forecasts because they are inaccurate
Use the same single-point approach as monthly forecasts and commit fully
Treat them as ranges or scenarios, review them regularly, and favour flexible decisions that can be adjusted as information improves
Average the monthly and three-year errors and assume 20% error for all horizons
questions.answer: Treat them as ranges or scenarios, review them regularly, and favour flexible decisions that can be adjusted as information improves
questions.explanation: Error grows with horizon, so long-term forecasts should express uncertainty and support flexible decisions. Abandoning them leaves strategic decisions with no basis at all.

questions.q: A multiplicative model has trend T = 200 + 5t (t in months) and a seasonal index of 0.90 for month t = 24. What is the forecast for month 24?
questions.explanation: Trend at t = 24 is 200 + 120 = 320; times 0.90 gives 288. 320 ignores seasonality, 319.1 subtracts the index additively and 355.6 divides by the index.

questions.q: Why is the forecast of total shampoo sales across all 40 SKUs usually more accurate (in percentage terms) than the forecasts for individual SKUs?
options: Random errors of individual SKUs partly offset each other when aggregated
The total uses a longer forecast horizon
Individual SKUs have no seasonality
Aggregated data always follow a straight-line trend
questions.answer: Random errors of individual SKUs partly offset each other when aggregated
questions.explanation: Aggregation pools independent random variation, so relative error falls. This is why long-range plans use aggregate forecasts.

questions.q: A store sold 1,500 units in December (seasonal index 1.5) and 1,100 units in February (seasonal index 0.9). Which month showed stronger underlying performance after removing seasonality?
options: December, because 1,500 is greater than 1,100
December, with deseasonalised sales of 2,250 units versus only 990 units for February
Both are equal once seasonality is removed
February, with deseasonalised sales of about 1,222 versus 1,000 for December
questions.answer: February, with deseasonalised sales of about 1,222 versus 1,000 for December
questions.explanation: 1,500/1.5 = 1,000 and 1,100/0.9 = 1,222. Comparing raw figures, or multiplying by the index, misses the seasonal adjustment.

questions.q: School-bag sales in Kerala have grown about 6% a year, spike every May-June before schools reopen, and dipped sharply during the 2018 floods. Which components are present?
options: Cyclical (the 6% annual growth), trend (the May-June spike) and seasonality (the 2018 floods)
Only seasonality, because school reopening drives everything
Trend (6% growth), seasonality (May-June spike) and an irregular component (2018 floods)
Trend (May-June spike), irregular (6% growth) and cyclical (floods)
questions.answer: Trend (6% growth), seasonality (May-June spike) and an irregular component (2018 floods)
questions.explanation: Steady growth is trend, a fixed annual spike is seasonal, and a one-off disaster is irregular. Mislabelling the annual spike as trend or the flood as cyclical are typical errors.

questions.q: Which combination of method and data granularity is most appropriate?
options: Short-term: Delphi expert panels and scenarios on annual aggregate data; long-term: exponential smoothing on daily SKU-level data
Short-term: exponential smoothing on weekly SKU-level data; long-term: judgemental or causal methods on annual aggregate data
Both horizons: a 3-month moving average on daily SKU data
Short-term: scenario planning on 10-year data; long-term: naive forecasts on hourly data
questions.answer: Short-term: exponential smoothing on weekly SKU-level data; long-term: judgemental or causal methods on annual aggregate data
questions.explanation: Short horizons need detailed, quick, data-driven methods; long horizons need aggregate data and judgement or causal reasoning. Swapping them mismatches method to decision.

references: A forecast can be classified by how far ahead it looks. Short-term forecasts cover days to about three months and support scheduling, ordering and staffing. Medium-term forecasts, roughly three months to three years, support aggregate production plans, budgets and hiring. Long-term forecasts, three years or more, support capacity, new plants, products and markets. Accuracy falls as the horizon lengthens, so long-term forecasts are made at an aggregate level and with more judgement. The data we forecast usually has components: a trend (long-run direction), seasonality (repeating pattern with a fixed period), cyclical movements (longer, irregular-length business cycles) and an irregular random part that cannot be predicted. Components can combine additively or multiplicatively.

Take a paint company like Asian Paints. Each week it forecasts SKU demand at depots to plan dispatches; this is short-term. Each year it forecasts quarterly volumes to set production plans and budgets; this is medium-term. For a new factory it forecasts demand five to ten years out; this is long-term and relies on aggregate trends and scenarios. When it studies past sales, it sees a growing trend, a seasonal peak before Diwali when people repaint homes, cyclical swings with the real-estate cycle, and random bumps from events like heavy rain. Separating these components helps forecast each properly, and the shorter the horizon, the more accurate the forecast usually is.

For managers, the key is matching the forecast to the decision. Short-term forecasts drive operational decisions such as inventory replenishment and shift rosters, and can use statistical methods on detailed data. Medium-term forecasts drive tactical decisions like aggregate planning, budgets and workforce levels. Long-term forecasts drive strategic decisions like capacity and market entry, and should be given as ranges or scenarios because uncertainty grows with the horizon. Understanding the components of a series helps: trend shows direction, seasonality tells us when peaks occur, cycles warn of economic swings, and the irregular part reminds us some error is unavoidable. Seasonal indices let us deseasonalise data to compare months fairly.

questions.q: In the forecasting process described by Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, what is the first step?
options: Choosing and fitting models
Gathering information
Using and evaluating the forecasting model
Problem definition
questions.answer: Problem definition
questions.explanation: The process starts by defining what is to be forecast, for whom and how it will be used. Jumping to model choice first is a common mistake.

questions.q: Which step comes immediately after problem definition in the forecasting process?
options: Choosing and fitting models
Evaluating forecast accuracy
Gathering information: data and the knowledge of people in the business
Preliminary (exploratory) analysis of the data to spot trends and outliers
questions.answer: Gathering information: data and the knowledge of people in the business
questions.explanation: After defining the problem, the forecaster gathers data and judgemental knowledge. Exploratory analysis needs that data first.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the preliminary (exploratory) analysis step?
options: To publish the final forecast to management and explain how it was produced
To graph the data and spot trends, seasonality and outliers before modelling
To set the sales target for next year
To collect opinions from customers
questions.answer: To graph the data and spot trends, seasonality and outliers before modelling
questions.explanation: Plotting and summarising data reveals patterns and problems that guide model choice. Publishing forecasts happens at the end of the process.

questions.q: What happens in the final step, 'using and evaluating a forecasting model'?
options: Forecasts are used for decisions and their accuracy is checked against actuals
The problem is defined and the users of the forecast are identified for the first time
Raw data are collected from databases
Outliers are identified by plotting the data
questions.answer: Forecasts are used for decisions and their accuracy is checked against actuals
questions.explanation: The last step closes the loop by comparing forecasts with actuals. Defining the problem and collecting data are earlier steps.

questions.q: Why is problem definition often described as the most difficult part of forecasting?
options: It involves the most complex mathematics of the whole process, such as estimating many model parameters and checking every statistical assumption
It requires the largest amount of data
It can only be done after the model is chosen
It requires understanding how the forecasts will be used, who needs them and how forecasting fits into the organisation
questions.answer: It requires understanding how the forecasts will be used, who needs them and how forecasting fits into the organisation
questions.explanation: Hyndman & Athanasopoulos note that defining the problem requires talking to everyone involved. The maths comes later and is often easier.

questions.q: Why do forecasters keep a 'test set' of recent data aside when building a model?
options: To give the model more data to fit, so that it matches the training period as closely as possible
To increase the amount of data used for fitting
To check accuracy on data the model has not seen, giving a realistic estimate of forecast error
To remove seasonality from the data
questions.answer: To check accuracy on data the model has not seen, giving a realistic estimate of forecast error
questions.explanation: Accuracy on fitted data is optimistic; a held-out test set mimics real forecasting. Using all data to fit makes evaluation unreliable.

questions.q: A sudden, lasting change in the pattern of a time series, for example after a major policy change, is called:
options: A seasonal index
A structural break
A moving average
A forecast horizon
questions.answer: A structural break
questions.explanation: A structural break means the old pattern no longer holds, a key forecasting challenge.

questions.q: An unusually high sales figure caused by a one-off bulk order from a single client is best described as:
options: An outlier
A trend
A seasonal pattern
A forecast horizon
questions.answer: An outlier
questions.explanation: An outlier is an observation far from the usual pattern. Treating it as trend would distort future forecasts.

questions.q: Why is input from domain experts (e.g., sales and marketing staff) valuable in the forecasting process?
options: They can replace all historical data, so statistical models are no longer needed once their opinions have been collected
They guarantee forecasts will be exactly right
They remove the need for evaluating accuracy
They know about upcoming events such as promotions, price changes or new competitors that are not in historical data
questions.answer: They know about upcoming events such as promotions, price changes or new competitors that are not in historical data
questions.explanation: Judgement adds information about the future that data cannot contain. Over-relying on it without checking bias is the opposite risk.

questions.q: Which is a common data challenge in forecasting?
options: Having too few forecasting textbooks
Using graphs during exploratory analysis, which tends to hide outliers and distort the patterns
Missing values, recording errors and changes in how data are defined over time
Reporting forecasts to managers
questions.answer: Missing values, recording errors and changes in how data are defined over time
questions.explanation: Real business data are messy; cleaning them is a large part of the process. Graphs are a tool for finding such problems, not the problem itself.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists the five basic steps of a forecasting task?
options: Gathering information, choosing models, problem definition, preliminary analysis, evaluating the model
Problem definition, gathering information, preliminary analysis, choosing and fitting models, using and evaluating the model
Choosing models, problem definition, gathering information, evaluating, preliminary analysis
Problem definition, choosing and fitting models, gathering information, evaluating, preliminary analysis
questions.answer: Problem definition, gathering information, preliminary analysis, choosing and fitting models, using and evaluating the model
questions.explanation: You must know the problem and see the data before choosing a model, and evaluation comes last. Choosing a model before exploring data is the typical error.

questions.q: A retailer's sales history understates true demand in weeks when products were out of stock. This challenge is known as:
options: Censored (constrained) demand: recorded sales are not equal to true demand during stock-outs
Seasonality in the data
Overfitting, because the model learns the stock-out weeks as if they were genuine low-demand weeks
A long forecast horizon
questions.answer: Censored (constrained) demand: recorded sales are not equal to true demand during stock-outs
questions.explanation: When shelves are empty, sales stop even if customers still want the product. Forecasting from raw sales then under-forecasts demand.

questions.q: An analyst plots three years of monthly sales and notices sharp spikes every October-November. In which step did this discovery happen, and what does it suggest?
options: Problem definition; it suggests the forecasting problem was wrongly defined and must be restated
Evaluation; it suggests the model is overfitting
Gathering information; it suggests the data are missing
Preliminary analysis; it suggests a seasonal (festive) pattern that the model must capture
questions.answer: Preliminary analysis; it suggests a seasonal (festive) pattern that the model must capture
questions.explanation: Exploratory graphs reveal patterns such as festive seasonality, which guide model selection.

questions.q: A firm has 36 months of data. It fits a model to the first 30 months and checks accuracy on the last 6. Why?
options: To make the model fit the first 30 months perfectly
Because the last 6 months are always outliers
To estimate how accurately the model forecasts data it has not seen
To remove the trend from the data
questions.answer: To estimate how accurately the model forecasts data it has not seen
questions.explanation: A holdout test mirrors real use, where the future is unknown. Judging accuracy on fitting data gives an over-optimistic picture.

questions.q: A week of very high sales was caused by a planned promotion. What is the best way to handle it when building a forecasting model?
options: Delete the week from the data without further checking, since unusual values always distort models and carry no useful information
Investigate the cause and model it explicitly (e.g., a promotion indicator) rather than blindly deleting or ignoring it
Treat it as normal demand and let it raise all future forecasts
Replace all data with the promotion week's value
questions.answer: Investigate the cause and model it explicitly (e.g., a promotion indicator) rather than blindly deleting or ignoring it
questions.explanation: Known causes such as promotions should be modelled so future promotions can be forecast. Blind deletion loses information; ignoring it inflates baseline forecasts.

questions.q: During problem definition for a sales forecast, who should the forecaster talk to?
options: The people who will use the forecasts and those who collect and maintain the data, such as sales, finance, operations and IT
Only the statistician who will build the model, since problem definition is mainly about choosing the right technique and software
Only external consultants
No one; problem definition is a purely technical task
questions.answer: The people who will use the forecasts and those who collect and maintain the data, such as sales, finance, operations and IT
questions.explanation: Problem definition requires understanding how forecasts will be used and what data exist. Treating it as purely technical leads to forecasts nobody can use.

questions.q: In the 'choosing and fitting models' step, the choice of model mainly depends on:
options: Whichever model is the most mathematically complex, since sophisticated models capture more patterns and so always forecast more accurately
The model used by the largest competitor
The manager's preferred target
The availability of historical data, the strength of relationships between variables and how the forecasts will be used
questions.answer: The availability of historical data, the strength of relationships between variables and how the forecasts will be used
questions.explanation: Model choice should fit the data and the decision. Complexity alone does not guarantee accuracy.

questions.q: Six months after a model goes live, its forecast errors begin growing steadily each month. What is the best response?
options: Ignore it, because errors always grow
Stop collecting actual data
Re-examine the model and data for changes in pattern, and refit or replace the model if needed
Keep the model unchanged, because it was accurate at launch and frequent changes confuse the planners who use it
questions.answer: Re-examine the model and data for changes in pattern, and refit or replace the model if needed
questions.explanation: Rising errors signal that conditions have changed. Ongoing evaluation exists precisely to catch this.

questions.q: Finance wants monthly revenue forecasts for budgeting while operations wants daily SKU-level forecasts for replenishment. What does this illustrate?
options: One forecast at a single level is always enough for everyone, so the finance team's monthly view should simply be adopted
Different users need different horizons and levels of detail, so the forecasting problem must be defined for each use
Finance and operations should not use forecasts
Only the operations forecast matters
questions.answer: Different users need different horizons and levels of detail, so the forecasting problem must be defined for each use
questions.explanation: Problem definition includes the horizon, frequency and aggregation each user needs. A single forecast rarely serves all decisions well.

questions.q: Why should a sophisticated forecasting model be compared with a simple benchmark such as the naive forecast?
options: To check that the added complexity actually improves accuracy
Because naive forecasts are always the most accurate
Because complex models cannot be evaluated directly
Because benchmarks remove seasonality
questions.answer: To check that the added complexity actually improves accuracy
questions.explanation: A model that cannot beat a naive benchmark is not worth its cost. Assuming the complex model must be better is the trap.

questions.q: A model achieves 2% MAPE on the training data but 18% MAPE on the test data. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is excellent, because a low training error shows it has captured all the patterns in the data
The test data must be wrong because the error is higher
The model is underfitting and needs fewer variables
The model is overfitting: it has fitted noise in the training data and does not generalise
questions.answer: The model is overfitting: it has fitted noise in the training data and does not generalise
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and test error is the classic sign of overfitting. Judging a model by its training fit is the main mistake.

questions.q: GST implementation in July 2017 changed how a distributor recorded and timed invoices, shifting the sales pattern. What is the best way to handle this in forecasting?
options: Ignore it, because more data always gives better forecasts
Delete all data after July 2017
Account for the break, for example by modelling it with an intervention variable, adjusting earlier data, or relying mainly on post-change data
Average pre- and post-GST data without adjustment
questions.answer: Account for the break, for example by modelling it with an intervention variable, adjusting earlier data, or relying mainly on post-change data
questions.explanation: A structural break means pre-change patterns may mislead. Ignoring it mixes two regimes; deleting post-change data discards the most relevant information.

questions.q: A store open 7 days a week sold 120 units of a product and stocked out at the end of day 3. Assuming demand is spread evenly across the week, what is the best estimate of unconstrained weekly demand?
options: 120 units
280 units
160 units
210 units
questions.answer: 280 units
questions.explanation: Daily demand is about 120 / 3 = 40, so weekly demand is about 40 x 7 = 280. Using 120 treats censored sales as true demand.

questions.q: Sales reps' bonuses depend on beating targets set from their own forecasts, and their forecasts are consistently too low. Which process safeguard is most effective?
options: Separate forecasting from target-setting and track each judgemental input's bias over time
Remove all statistical forecasts and rely only on the reps
Increase every forecast by a random amount
Stop measuring forecast accuracy to avoid conflict
questions.answer: Separate forecasting from target-setting and track each judgemental input's bias over time
questions.explanation: Incentives create deliberate bias (sandbagging). Decoupling forecasts from rewards and monitoring bias addresses the cause.

questions.q: A grocery chain has 10 years of data, but quick-commerce apps changed customer buying patterns two years ago. What is the most sensible data strategy?
options: Use all 10 years equally, because more data always means better forecasts
Use only data from before quick commerce, because it is more stable
Use no data and rely on the CEO's target
Give more weight to recent data (or use mainly post-change data), accepting fewer observations in exchange for relevance
questions.answer: Give more weight to recent data (or use mainly post-change data), accepting fewer observations in exchange for relevance
questions.explanation: When the pattern has changed, relevance beats volume. Older data reflect a market that no longer exists.

questions.q: A bank asks its analytics team to 'forecast cash demand'. What is the most important clarification before any modelling?
options: Which forecasting software has the best user interface
Whether the forecast should use the most complex model available
Which ATMs or branches, at what frequency and horizon, and how the forecast will drive cash replenishment decisions
Whether forecast errors should be hidden from management
questions.answer: Which ATMs or branches, at what frequency and horizon, and how the forecast will drive cash replenishment decisions
questions.explanation: Problem definition fixes the level, horizon and use of the forecast. Choosing software or models first puts tools before the problem.

questions.q: During exploration, an analyst finds that sales were recorded in lakhs of rupees until 2020 and in rupees afterwards. What should be done?
options: Model the data as-is, since the model will detect the change automatically
Convert the data to consistent units before modelling; otherwise the model will see a false structural break
Treat the post-2020 values as outliers and delete them
Average the two periods to smooth the difference
questions.answer: Convert the data to consistent units before modelling; otherwise the model will see a false structural break
questions.explanation: Inconsistent units create artificial jumps that look like a huge increase. Harmonising definitions is essential data preparation.

questions.q: Test-period actual sales are 100, 110, 105 and 120 units (the last training value was 95). A one-step naive forecast uses the previous actual each month. A new model forecast 102, 108, 110 and 112. Using MAE, does the new model beat the naive benchmark?
options: Yes: model MAE = 4.25 versus naive MAE = 8.75
No: model MAE = 8.75 versus naive MAE = 4.25
Yes: model MAE = 17 versus naive MAE = 35
They are equal: both have MAE = 4.25
questions.answer: Yes: model MAE = 4.25 versus naive MAE = 8.75
questions.explanation: Naive forecasts are 95, 100, 110, 105, giving errors 5, 10, 5, 15 (MAE 8.75). Model errors are 2, 2, 5, 8 (MAE 4.25). 17 and 35 are sums of absolute errors, not averages.

questions.q: Why is time series cross-validation (rolling forecast origin) preferred over random k-fold cross-validation for forecasting models?
options: Random k-fold always gives a lower error estimate, which makes every model look misleadingly good regardless of its true forecasting ability
Time series cross-validation uses less computing power
Random k-fold cannot be used with more than 100 observations
Each forecast must be made using only data from before the forecast period; random folds let future information leak into training
questions.answer: Each forecast must be made using only data from before the forecast period; random folds let future information leak into training
questions.explanation: Forecasting respects time order; mixing future and past observations flatters accuracy. The point is avoiding information leakage, not computing cost.

questions.q: An e-commerce company must forecast weekly demand for 5,000 SKUs with a team of three analysts. What is the most practical approach?
options: Have analysts hand-build a complex custom model for each SKU
Forecast only the top 10 SKUs and ignore the rest
Use an automated, simple and robust method for all SKUs, and focus analyst judgement on high-value or volatile SKUs
Use the same fixed number for every SKU
questions.answer: Use an automated, simple and robust method for all SKUs, and focus analyst judgement on high-value or volatile SKUs
questions.explanation: At scale, automation with targeted judgement is the realistic choice. Custom models for 5,000 SKUs are infeasible, and ignoring SKUs leaves stocking decisions blind.

references: Forecasting follows a process. First, define the problem: what exactly is forecast, at what level, for which horizon and for which decision. Second, gather information, meaning historical data plus the knowledge of people in sales, marketing and operations. Third, do preliminary analysis by plotting the data to see trend, seasonality, outliers and relationships. Fourth, choose and fit candidate models and compare them, including with simple benchmarks. Fifth, use the forecasts and evaluate them against actual results, updating the model when it drifts. Common challenges include poor or missing data, outliers, sales data that hide true demand during stock-outs, structural breaks such as GST, overfitting, and biased judgement.

Suppose a hotel chain wants to forecast room demand. We first ask who needs it: revenue managers want daily forecasts for pricing, while finance wants monthly totals. Then we collect booking history and talk to sales teams about upcoming conferences. Plotting the data shows weekend peaks, a December season and some odd spikes from one-off events. We try a few models, keeping the last few months aside as a test set to see which really forecasts best, and compare against a naive forecast. Once in use, we track errors every month. Challenges include COVID-like breaks, data errors, outliers, and sales staff padding their forecasts to hit targets.

For a manager, the forecasting process is a cycle, not a one-time calculation. It starts with clear problem definition, because a forecast at the wrong level or horizon is useless however accurate. Next comes gathering data and expert judgement, then exploratory analysis to understand patterns and clean the data. Only then do we select and fit models, judging them on held-out test data rather than on how well they fit the past, to avoid overfitting. Finally, we use the forecast for decisions and monitor accuracy, refitting when patterns change. The main challenges are data quality, censored demand, structural change, judgemental bias and limited analyst time across many products.

topics.topic: Role of Forecasting in Managerial Planning and Control

questions.q: In managerial planning, forecasts are mainly used to:
options: Set budgets, production plans and staffing levels
Record last year's transactions for the statutory audit
Replace the need for any control or performance review
Fix the share price of the company on the stock exchange
questions.answer: Set budgets, production plans and staffing levels
questions.explanation: Plans need an estimate of future demand and costs, which forecasts provide. Forecasts do not replace control; they feed it.

questions.q: In management, 'control' refers to:
options: Preparing a forecast for the first time without any reference to past data or plans
Setting a long-term vision statement for the company
Hiring new staff whenever sales increase
Comparing actual results with plans or forecasts and taking corrective action
questions.answer: Comparing actual results with plans or forecasts and taking corrective action
questions.explanation: Control closes the loop: measure actuals, compare with plan, investigate deviations, and act.

questions.q: Which forecast is usually the starting point of a company's annual master budget?
options: The capital expenditure forecast for new machinery
The forecast of employee attrition
The sales forecast
The forecast of tax refunds due
questions.answer: The sales forecast
questions.explanation: Production, purchase, labour and cash budgets are all derived from expected sales. Starting elsewhere leaves those budgets without a demand basis.

questions.q: In budgetary control, a variance is:
options: The average of all forecasts made during the year
The difference between the actual result and the budgeted or forecast figure
The sales target set by the board
The number of months in the planning horizon
questions.answer: The difference between the actual result and the budgeted or forecast figure
questions.explanation: Variance analysis is the core control tool: actual minus budget, investigated when large.

questions.q: Demand forecasts and their error are used in inventory management mainly to set:
options: Reorder points and safety stock
Employee salaries and annual bonuses
The company's dividend policy
The rate of income tax payable
questions.answer: Reorder points and safety stock
questions.explanation: Reorder levels cover expected lead-time demand and safety stock covers forecast error.

questions.q: Capacity planning, such as adding a new production line, mainly relies on:
options: Tomorrow's sales forecast for each store
Hourly website traffic forecasts
Next week's delivery schedule
Long-term demand forecasts
questions.answer: Long-term demand forecasts
questions.explanation: Capacity takes years to add and lasts years, so it needs long-range forecasts.

questions.q: A hospital uses patient-volume forecasts to decide how many nurses to roster each shift. This is an example of forecasting supporting:
options: Capital structure decisions
Brand positioning strategy
Workforce (staff) planning
Statutory financial reporting
questions.answer: Workforce (staff) planning
questions.explanation: Staffing is set ahead of demand, so it depends on forecasts of workload.

questions.q: A cash flow forecast mainly helps a business to:
options: Calculate the depreciation on fixed assets for the balance sheet
Anticipate cash shortfalls or surpluses and arrange funds in advance
Decide the colour scheme of its packaging
Measure customer satisfaction scores
questions.answer: Anticipate cash shortfalls or surpluses and arrange funds in advance
questions.explanation: Cash forecasts reveal when borrowing or investing will be needed, avoiding liquidity crises.

questions.q: The tracking signal in forecast control is used to:
options: Detect persistent bias in a forecast
Measure the share price of the company
Calculate the seasonal index for each month
Rank employees by their sales performance
questions.answer: Detect persistent bias in a forecast
questions.explanation: Tracking signal = cumulative forecast error / MAD; large values show forecasts are consistently too high or too low.

questions.q: A rolling forecast is one that:
options: Is prepared once a year and never changed
Covers only the remaining months of the current financial year, shrinking as the year passes
Uses only the previous month's actual value
Is updated regularly and always extends a fixed period ahead, such as the next 12 months
questions.answer: Is updated regularly and always extends a fixed period ahead, such as the next 12 months
questions.explanation: Rolling forecasts add a new period each time one passes, keeping a constant look-ahead. A static annual budget shrinks toward year-end.

questions.q: The running sum of forecast errors (RSFE, actual minus forecast) is 30 units and the mean absolute deviation (MAD) is 10 units. What is the tracking signal?
questions.explanation: Tracking signal = RSFE / MAD = 30 / 10 = 3.0. 0.33 inverts the ratio and 300 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: A firm uses control limits of +/-4 MAD. The tracking signal (errors = actual minus forecast) is +5.2. What should management conclude?
options: The forecast is in control because the signal is positive
The forecast is out of control and is consistently under-forecasting demand
The forecast is out of control and is consistently over-forecasting customer demand
The forecast is unbiased, but its errors are very small
questions.answer: The forecast is out of control and is consistently under-forecasting demand
questions.explanation: A signal beyond +4 indicates bias. With errors defined as actual minus forecast, a positive signal means actuals keep exceeding forecasts, i.e., under-forecasting.

questions.q: Weekly demand forecast error has a standard deviation of 40 units, lead time is 1 week, and the firm wants a 95% service level (z = 1.65). What safety stock is required?
options: 66 units
40 units
24.2 units
106 units
questions.answer: 66 units
questions.explanation: Safety stock = z x sigma = 1.65 x 40 = 66. 24.2 divides by z, and 106 adds z-adjusted and raw values.

questions.q: A firm budgeted sales of 5,000 units at Rs 200 each, but sold 4,600 units at Rs 200. What is the sales revenue variance?
options: Rs 80,000 favourable
Rs 400 adverse
Rs 9,20,000 adverse
Rs 80,000 adverse
questions.answer: Rs 80,000 adverse
questions.explanation: (4,600 - 5,000) x 200 = -80,000, an adverse variance. Rs 400 is the unit shortfall without the price, and 9,20,000 is actual revenue.

questions.q: A hotel forecasts 180 occupied rooms tomorrow. Each housekeeper can clean 12 rooms per shift. How many housekeepers should be scheduled?
questions.explanation: 180 / 12 = 15 housekeepers. 2,160 multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: A business has an opening cash balance of Rs 10 lakh, forecast inflows of Rs 25 lakh, outflows of Rs 32 lakh, and must keep a minimum balance of Rs 5 lakh. How much must it arrange to borrow?
options: Rs 7 lakh
Rs 2 lakh
Rs 3 lakh
Nothing; the closing balance is positive
questions.answer: Rs 2 lakh
questions.explanation: Closing cash = 10 + 25 - 32 = 3 lakh, which is 2 lakh below the 5 lakh minimum. Rs 7 lakh ignores the opening balance; 'nothing' ignores the minimum.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a rolling 12-month forecast over a static annual budget?
options: It incorporates new information regularly, so plans stay relevant as conditions change
It never needs to be revised once it has been approved by the board
It guarantees that actual results will match the plan each month
It removes the need to compare actual results with plans
questions.answer: It incorporates new information regularly, so plans stay relevant as conditions change
questions.explanation: Rolling forecasts are updated with each new period of data. Static budgets become stale as the year progresses.

questions.q: Under 'management by exception', how should a manager use forecast-versus-actual reports?
options: Investigate every rupee of difference between actual and forecast with equal effort
Ignore all deviations, because forecasts are always imperfect
Change the forecast so that it always equals the actual figure
Focus attention on deviations that are large or persistent
questions.answer: Focus attention on deviations that are large or persistent
questions.explanation: Control effort should go to significant deviations. Chasing every small variance wastes time; ignoring all of them abandons control.

questions.q: Actual monthly sales have fallen 15% below forecast for three months in a row. What is the appropriate control response?
options: Keep the original forecast unchanged until the year-end review
Increase production to make up for the lower sales
Investigate the causes, then revise the forecast and adjust production and purchase plans
Stop forecasting until sales recover to the old level
questions.answer: Investigate the causes, then revise the forecast and adjust production and purchase plans
questions.explanation: Persistent deviations signal a changed situation; control means diagnosing and updating plans. Holding the old forecast builds excess inventory.

questions.q: A company forecasts demand of 12,000 units next quarter, has opening inventory of 2,000 units and wants closing inventory of 3,000 units. What production is required?
options: 11,000 units
13,000 units
12,000 units
17,000 units
questions.answer: 13,000 units
questions.explanation: Production = demand + desired closing - opening = 12,000 + 3,000 - 2,000 = 13,000. 11,000 reverses the inventory adjustment; 17,000 adds both inventories.

questions.q: Monthly forecast errors (actual minus forecast) for six months are +8, +12, -4, +10, +6, +10. Control limits are +/-4 MAD. What is the tracking signal and conclusion?
options: 5.04; it exceeds +4, so the forecast is persistently too low
0.84; it is well within limits, so no action is needed
5.04; it is within limits, so the forecast is in control
4.20; it exceeds +4, so the forecast is persistently too high
questions.answer: 5.04; it exceeds +4, so the forecast is persistently too low
questions.explanation: RSFE = 42 and MAD = 50/6 = 8.33, so TS = 42/8.33 = 5.04, beyond +4. Positive errors mean actual exceeds forecast (under-forecasting). 0.84 divides by the sum of absolute errors instead of MAD.

questions.q: A distributor forecasts 400 units of weekly demand. Weekly forecast error has standard deviation 50 units, lead time is 4 weeks, and z = 1.65. Assuming independent weekly errors, what is the reorder point?
options: 1,930 units
1,682.5 units
1,600 units
1,765 units
questions.answer: 1,765 units
questions.explanation: Lead-time demand = 4 x 400 = 1,600; lead-time sigma = 50 x sqrt(4) = 100; safety stock = 165; ROP = 1,765. 1,930 scales sigma by 4 instead of sqrt(4); 1,682.5 ignores lead time in the sigma.

questions.q: A consumer-durables firm's forecasts have been about 10% too high for every month this year, leading to excess stock and blocked working capital. What is the best corrective action?
options: Keep the forecasts and simply add warehouse space for the extra stock it creates
Hold larger safety stocks to protect against the inaccurate forecasts
Identify and correct the source of the bias in the forecasting process
Ignore it, since a 10% error is within the normal range for durables
questions.answer: Identify and correct the source of the bias in the forecasting process
questions.explanation: A consistent one-direction error is bias, which can be removed at source. Adding buffers treats a symptom and makes overstock worse.

questions.q: Budgeted variable cost is Rs 50 per unit on a forecast of 10,000 units. Actual output was 9,000 units with actual variable cost of Rs 4,80,000. What is the correct cost variance for control?
options: Rs 20,000 favourable, because actual cost is below the original budget of Rs 5,00,000
Rs 30,000 adverse against the flexible budget, though it looks Rs 20,000 favourable against the static budget
Rs 30,000 favourable against the flexible budget of Rs 4,50,000
Rs 80,000 adverse against the static budget
questions.answer: Rs 30,000 adverse against the flexible budget, though it looks Rs 20,000 favourable against the static budget
questions.explanation: Flexible budget = 9,000 x 50 = 4,50,000, so actual 4,80,000 is 30,000 adverse. Comparing with the static 5,00,000 wrongly credits the manager for lower volume.

questions.q: A Jaipur hotel's demand forecast for a wedding-season weekend is well above capacity, while a mid-week in July is forecast at 40% occupancy. How should revenue managers use these forecasts?
options: Raise rates and restrict discounts on the peak weekend; offer promotions and packages for the low mid-week
Keep the same rates on both dates, because forecasts should not influence pricing decisions
Offer deep discounts on the peak weekend to build customer loyalty for the future
Close the hotel mid-week and run at full price only on weekends
questions.answer: Raise rates and restrict discounts on the peak weekend; offer promotions and packages for the low mid-week
questions.explanation: Revenue management uses demand forecasts to set prices and inventory controls. Discounting when demand exceeds capacity gives away revenue.

questions.q: A firm forecasts demand in five years of between 80,000 and 1,20,000 units per year. Options: build a 1,20,000-unit plant now, or build 80,000 units now with space to expand. What is the soundest approach?
options: Build 1,20,000 units now, because capacity is cheaper to build in one step than in two
Build 1,00,000 units now, because it is the midpoint of the forecast range
Postpone all capacity decisions until demand is known with certainty
Build 80,000 units with an expansion option, triggered when demand signals confirm growth
questions.answer: Build 80,000 units with an expansion option, triggered when demand signals confirm growth
questions.explanation: With a wide forecast range, flexibility reduces the risk of idle capacity while keeping upside. Waiting for certainty means losing sales, and building for the top end risks large idle cost.

questions.q: Forecast errors (actual minus forecast) over four weeks are +10, -10, +10, -10. What do the tracking signal and MAD tell the manager?
options: TS = 4, so the forecast is biased upward and should be corrected
TS = 0 and MAD = 0, so the forecast is perfect
TS = 0, so there is no bias, but MAD = 10 units may still be too large for planning
TS = 1, so the forecast is under-forecasting slightly every week
questions.answer: TS = 0, so there is no bias, but MAD = 10 units may still be too large for planning
questions.explanation: RSFE = 0 so TS = 0 (unbiased), while MAD = 10. Being unbiased is not the same as being accurate; treating TS = 0 as perfect is the main error.

questions.q: What is the main role of the forecast in a Sales and Operations Planning (S&OP) process?
options: Each department keeps its own separate forecast so that every team can meet its own targets
It provides one consensus demand plan that sales, operations and finance align their plans to
The forecast is used only by the finance team to report last month's results
It replaces the need for operations to plan capacity
questions.answer: It provides one consensus demand plan that sales, operations and finance align their plans to
questions.explanation: S&OP reconciles demand and supply around one agreed forecast each month. Separate departmental numbers are exactly the problem it solves.

questions.q: A bank's call centre forecasts 4,800 calls per day. Each agent handles 60 calls per shift, and 20% of rostered agents are typically unavailable (leave, training). How many agents should be rostered?
questions.explanation: Productive agents needed = 4,800 / 60 = 80; rostered = 80 / (1 - 0.20) = 100. 96 adds 20% to 80, which under-covers shrinkage; 64 subtracts it.

questions.q: In the first 3 days of a 10-day festive sale, an e-commerce firm's electronics sales run 30% above forecast. What is the best control action?
options: Keep the original forecast unchanged, because sale forecasts should only be reviewed afterwards
Assume the 30% uplift will continue for the whole year and raise annual plans
Cut prices further to push sales even higher
Reforecast the remaining days with the new data and reallocate stock, checking if demand is merely pulled forward
questions.answer: Reforecast the remaining days with the new data and reallocate stock, checking if demand is merely pulled forward
questions.explanation: Early actuals are valuable information; control means updating forecasts and reallocating inventory. Extrapolating a festival spike to the whole year is a typical error.
