references: Planning means deciding in advance what to do, and every plan rests on a forecast. The sales forecast drives the budget, production plan, purchasing, inventory levels, staffing and cash requirements, while long-term forecasts drive capacity and investment. Control means comparing actual results with these plans, analysing variances and taking corrective action. Forecasting supports control in two ways: it sets the benchmark against which actuals are judged, and forecast errors themselves are monitored, for example using a tracking signal, to detect bias. When deviations are large or persistent, managers investigate, update the forecast and adjust plans. Rolling forecasts keep this planning and control cycle current.

Consider a hotel chain. Its forecast of room nights for the next quarter sets the revenue budget, decides how many housekeepers and chefs to roster, and guides room pricing: higher rates when demand exceeds capacity, discounts when it is weak. The finance team uses the same forecast for cash planning. Each month, actual occupancy is compared with the forecast. If actuals keep falling short, the variance is investigated, the forecast is revised and staffing and purchases are cut. A tracking signal shows whether forecasts are consistently too high or too low. So forecasting is the starting point of planning and the yardstick for control.

For managers, forecasting links planning and control in a continuous loop: forecast, plan, act, measure, compare and correct. Short-term forecasts set inventory reorder points, safety stock and shift rosters; medium-term forecasts set budgets and aggregate production plans; long-term forecasts guide capacity and strategy. Control uses variance analysis, management by exception and flexible budgets to judge performance fairly. Forecast errors also need control: a tracking signal outside its limits signals bias that should be fixed at source rather than covered with extra stock. Processes like S&OP align sales, operations and finance around one forecast, and rolling forecasts keep plans updated as new information arrives.

topics.topic: Forecast Accuracy: MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE

questions.q: MAE stands for:
options: Maximum Average Error
Mean Absolute Error
Mean Adjusted Estimate
Median Absolute Error
questions.answer: Mean Absolute Error
questions.explanation: MAE is the average of the absolute forecast errors. 'Median' absolute error is a different, less common measure.

questions.q: Which accuracy measure is expressed as a percentage of the actual values?
options: MAPE
MAE
MSE
RMSE
questions.answer: MAPE
questions.explanation: MAPE averages |error| / actual x 100. MAE, MSE and RMSE are in the units (or squared units) of the data.

questions.q: RMSE is calculated as:
options: The square of the mean absolute error
The mean of the square roots of the absolute errors
The mean absolute error divided by the mean of actuals
The square root of the mean squared error
questions.answer: The square root of the mean squared error
questions.explanation: RMSE = sqrt(MSE), which brings the measure back to the original units. Squaring MAE is a common confusion.

questions.q: Forecast error for a period is usually defined as:
options: Forecast value minus the previous period's forecast
Actual value divided by forecast value
Actual value minus forecast value
Forecast value plus actual value
questions.answer: Actual value minus forecast value
questions.explanation: e = A - F is the standard definition (Hyndman uses y minus y-hat). A ratio of actual to forecast is not an error measure.

questions.q: Which measure penalises large errors most heavily because it squares them?
options: MAE
MSE
MAPE
Mean error (bias)
questions.answer: MSE
questions.explanation: Squaring makes a 10-unit error count 100 and a 2-unit error count 4. MAE weights errors linearly.

questions.q: If demand is measured in units, MSE is expressed in:
options: Squared units
Units
Percentage
It has no units at all
questions.answer: Squared units
questions.explanation: MSE averages squared errors, so its unit is units squared. RMSE returns to the original units.

questions.q: What happens to MAPE when an actual value in the data is zero?
options: It becomes exactly zero
It equals the MAE
It is unaffected by that period
It becomes undefined (division by zero)
questions.answer: It becomes undefined (division by zero)
questions.explanation: MAPE divides by the actual value, so a zero actual makes it undefined or infinite. This is a key weakness for intermittent demand.

questions.q: When comparing two forecasting methods on the same data, a lower MAE indicates:
options: Worse accuracy on average
More forecast bias
Better accuracy on average
A longer forecast horizon
questions.answer: Better accuracy on average
questions.explanation: Error measures are 'smaller is better'. Lower MAE means forecasts were closer to actuals on average.

questions.q: Which measure is best for comparing forecast accuracy across products measured in different units (e.g., litres of milk and number of TVs)?
options: MAE
MAPE
MSE
RMSE
questions.answer: MAPE
questions.explanation: MAPE is a percentage, so it is scale-independent. MAE, MSE and RMSE depend on the units of the data.

questions.q: With error defined as actual minus forecast, a consistently positive error means the forecast is:
options: Too low (under-forecasting)
Too high (over-forecasting)
Perfectly accurate
Unbiased but noisy
questions.answer: Too low (under-forecasting)
questions.explanation: Positive A - F means actual exceeded forecast, so forecasts were too low. Reversing the sign convention is the common slip.

questions.q: Actual sales for three weeks were 100, 120 and 110 units; forecasts were 90, 125 and 110. What is the MAE?
options: 1.67 units
41.67 units
15 units
5 units
questions.answer: 5 units
questions.explanation: Absolute errors are 10, 5, 0; MAE = 15/3 = 5. 1.67 averages signed errors (10 - 5 + 0)/3, and 15 is the sum rather than the mean.

questions.q: Actual sales for three weeks were 100, 120 and 110 units; forecasts were 90, 125 and 110. What is the MSE?
questions.explanation: Squared errors are 100, 25, 0; MSE = 125/3 = 41.67. 6.45 is the RMSE and 125 is the sum of squares without averaging.

questions.q: A forecasting model has an MSE of 64 (units squared). What is its RMSE?
options: 32 units
8 units
4,096 units
16 units
questions.answer: 8 units
questions.explanation: RMSE = sqrt(64) = 8. 32 halves instead of square-rooting, and 4,096 squares again.

questions.q: A supermarket's actual sales of rice were 200 kg and the forecast was 180 kg. What is the absolute percentage error for this period?
questions.explanation: |200 - 180| / 200 x 100 = 10%. Dividing by the forecast (20/180) gives 11.11%, a common mistake.

questions.q: Actual demand for three periods was 50, 100 and 200 units; forecasts were 45, 110 and 190. What is the MAPE?
questions.explanation: APEs are 10%, 10% and 5%; mean = 8.33%. 7.14% is total absolute error / total actual (a weighted measure), 8.49% divides by forecasts, and 25% sums APEs.

questions.q: A sales forecast has a MAPE of 4%. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Exactly 4% of the forecasts were wrong and the rest were perfect
The forecasts were on average 4 units away from actual sales
On average, the forecasts were off by about 4% of actual sales
The forecasts were biased upward by about 4% of actual sales
questions.answer: On average, the forecasts were off by about 4% of actual sales
questions.explanation: MAPE is the average absolute percentage error. It says nothing about direction (bias), and it is not in units.

questions.q: Method A has MAE 10 and RMSE 11; Method B has MAE 9 and RMSE 15 on the same data. What does this suggest?
options: A is better on every measure, so B's lower MAE must be a calculation error in the report
B is slightly better on average but makes some large errors, as its RMSE is far above its MAE
B is better on every measure, since it has the lower MAE of the two methods
Both methods are equally accurate, because their MAE values are so similar
questions.answer: B is slightly better on average but makes some large errors, as its RMSE is far above its MAE
questions.explanation: RMSE much greater than MAE signals a few big errors. Which method to prefer depends on whether big errors are especially costly.

questions.q: Errors (actual minus forecast) over four months were +5, -3, +4 and +6. What is the mean error and what does it indicate?
options: Mean error = 3; the forecast tends to under-predict demand
Mean error = 4.5; the forecast tends to over-predict demand
Mean error = 3; the forecast tends to over-predict demand
Mean error = 12; the forecast is unbiased overall
questions.answer: Mean error = 3; the forecast tends to under-predict demand
questions.explanation: (5 - 3 + 4 + 6)/4 = 3. A positive mean error (A - F) means actuals exceed forecasts, i.e., under-forecasting. 4.5 is the MAE, and 12 is the sum.

questions.q: Errors over four periods are +4, -4, +4 and -4. What are the MAE and RMSE?
options: MAE = 0 and RMSE = 4
MAE = 4 and RMSE = 16
MAE = 4 and RMSE = 2
MAE = 4 and RMSE = 4
questions.answer: MAE = 4 and RMSE = 4
questions.explanation: All absolute errors equal 4, so MAE = 4 and RMSE = sqrt(16) = 4. RMSE equals MAE only when all errors have the same size; 0 is the mean signed error, and 16 is the MSE.

questions.q: A hotel's room-night forecast has an MSE of 900. What is the RMSE and in what units?
options: 900 room-nights
30 percent
30 room-nights
450 room-nights squared
questions.answer: 30 room-nights
questions.explanation: RMSE = sqrt(900) = 30, in the original units (room-nights). MSE itself is in squared units, and RMSE is not a percentage.

questions.q: Actual weekly sales were 200, 220, 210, 230. Method X forecast 210, 210, 220, 220; Method Y forecast 200, 220, 210, 254. Which method does each measure prefer?
options: Both prefer Y (MAE 6 vs 10; RMSE 6 vs 10)
MAE prefers Y (6 vs 10); RMSE prefers X (10 vs 12)
MAE prefers X (10 vs 6); RMSE prefers Y (12 vs 10)
Both prefer X (MAE 10 vs 12; RMSE 10 vs 12)
questions.answer: MAE prefers Y (6 vs 10); RMSE prefers X (10 vs 12)
questions.explanation: X errors: -10, 10, -10, 10 (MAE 10, RMSE 10). Y errors: 0, 0, 0, -24 (MAE 6, RMSE sqrt(576/4) = 12). RMSE punishes Y's single large miss.

questions.q: A slow-moving SKU had actual sales of 2, 50 and 100 units, with forecasts 4, 48 and 95. What is the MAPE, and why can it mislead?
options: 36.33%; it is inflated by the 100% error in the low-volume period
5.92%; MAPE weights each period by its sales volume
19.81%; it is inflated by the low-volume first period
3.00%; the error is small, so the forecast is clearly excellent
questions.answer: 36.33%; it is inflated by the 100% error in the low-volume period
questions.explanation: APEs are 100%, 4% and 5%, so MAPE = 36.33%. A 2-unit miss on a tiny base dominates. 5.92% is total error/total actual, 19.81% divides by forecasts, and 3.00 is the MAE in units.

questions.q: Actual monthly sales (Rs lakh) were 500, 520, 480, 510, 530; forecasts were 490, 530, 500, 500, 520. What is the RMSE?
options: Rs 160 lakh
Rs 12 lakh
Rs 28.28 lakh
Rs 12.65 lakh
questions.answer: Rs 12.65 lakh
questions.explanation: Errors 10, -10, -20, 10, 10; squares sum to 800; MSE = 160; RMSE = 12.65. 160 is the MSE, 12 is the MAE and 28.28 is the square root of the sum without averaging.

questions.q: SKU A (soap) has mean weekly demand 10,000 units and MAE 500. SKU B (premium shampoo) has mean demand 200 units and MAE 50. Which is forecast better relative to its volume?
options: SKU B, because its MAE of 50 units is ten times smaller than SKU A's
SKU A, because its MAE of 500 units is ten times larger than SKU B's
SKU A, as its error is about 5% of demand versus 25% for SKU B
Both are equally good, because MAE cannot be compared across products
questions.answer: SKU A, as its error is about 5% of demand versus 25% for SKU B
questions.explanation: Relative error is 500/10,000 = 5% for A and 50/200 = 25% for B. Comparing raw MAE across different scales is misleading.

questions.q: A sweet shop's forecast errors over five weeks were 5, 5, 5, 5 and 60 units (the last during Diwali). What is the RMSE and what does it reveal?
options: 16 units; it equals the MAE, so all of the errors are of a similar size
27.20 units; it is far above the MAE of 16, showing one large error dominates
740 units; it is far above the MAE, so the forecast is completely unusable
27.20 units; it is close to the MAE, so the weekly errors are consistent
questions.answer: 27.20 units; it is far above the MAE of 16, showing one large error dominates
questions.explanation: Squares: 4 x 25 + 3,600 = 3,700; MSE = 740; RMSE = 27.20, versus MAE = 80/5 = 16. A large RMSE-MAE gap flags occasional big misses.

questions.q: A bank stocks cash in ATMs. Small forecast misses are cheap, but a large shortfall (ATM running dry) causes big costs and complaints. Which measure should guide model choice?
options: RMSE (or MSE), as squaring makes large errors weigh much more heavily
MAPE, because percentage errors are always the most useful measure for managers
MAE, because it treats every unit of error equally regardless of its size
Mean error, because only the overall bias matters for cash planning
questions.answer: RMSE (or MSE), as squaring makes large errors weigh much more heavily
questions.explanation: When large errors are disproportionately costly, a squared-error measure aligns with the business cost. MAE treats big and small misses linearly.

questions.q: Case 1: actual 100, forecast 150. Case 2: actual 150, forecast 100. Both have an absolute error of 50. What are the absolute percentage errors?
options: 50% in both cases, because the absolute error is 50 units in each case
33.33% and 50%; MAPE penalises under-forecasts more at the same absolute error
50% and 66.67%; MAPE divides the absolute error by the forecast value
50% and 33.33%; MAPE penalises over-forecasts more at the same absolute error
questions.answer: 50% and 33.33%; MAPE penalises over-forecasts more at the same absolute error
questions.explanation: 50/100 = 50% and 50/150 = 33.33%. Dividing by the actual makes over-forecasts on small actuals look worse, a known asymmetry of MAPE.

questions.q: Method P has errors +10, +10, +10, +10. Method Q has errors +15, -15, +15, -15. Which statement is correct?
options: P is better on every count, because its errors are smaller and also perfectly consistent
Q is better on every count, because its mean error of zero shows it is the more accurate
Q is unbiased but less accurate (MAE 15 vs 10); adding 10 to P's forecasts would remove its bias
Both methods are equally good, because their mean errors are both less than 15 units
questions.answer: Q is unbiased but less accurate (MAE 15 vs 10); adding 10 to P's forecasts would remove its bias
questions.explanation: P: mean error 10, MAE 10 (biased). Q: mean error 0, MAE 15 (unbiased, noisier). Correcting P's constant bias would make its errors zero, so bias and accuracy must be judged separately.

questions.q: Over five months, a forecast's MAE was 6 units. In the sixth month the absolute error was 18 units. What is the new MAE over six months?
options: 12 units
8 units
9.6 units
24 units
questions.answer: 8 units
questions.explanation: Total absolute error = 5 x 6 + 18 = 48; 48/6 = 8. 12 averages the two MAEs, and 9.6 divides by 5 instead of 6.

questions.q: An auto spare-parts dealer has many months with zero demand for slow-moving parts. Which accuracy measure is most appropriate?
options: MAE (or a scaled measure such as MASE), as MAPE is undefined when demand is zero
MAPE, because it is scale-free and therefore suits every kind of demand pattern
MAPE, after deleting the zero-demand months from the data before calculation
No measure can be used, because intermittent demand cannot be evaluated
questions.answer: MAE (or a scaled measure such as MASE), as MAPE is undefined when demand is zero
questions.explanation: Zero actuals make MAPE undefined; deleting them hides real errors. Absolute or scaled measures work with intermittent demand.

references: Forecast accuracy tells us how close forecasts are to actual values. The forecast error is actual minus forecast. MAE, the mean absolute error, averages the absolute errors and is easy to explain because it is in the same units as the data. MSE, the mean squared error, averages squared errors, so it penalises large errors heavily but is in squared units. RMSE is the square root of MSE, returning to the original units while still emphasising big misses; it is always at least as large as MAE. MAPE averages absolute errors as a percentage of actuals, so it is scale-independent and useful for comparing products, but it breaks down when actual values are zero or very small.

Suppose a retail store forecast 90, 125 and 110 units and actually sold 100, 120 and 110. The errors are 10, -5 and 0. MAE is 5 units, meaning we were off by 5 units on average. MSE is 41.67 and RMSE about 6.45 units, a bit higher because the 10-unit miss is weighted more. If the errors are expressed as percentages of actual sales, the MAPE is about 4.7%, which lets us compare this store with a much larger one. If a forecast has one huge Diwali miss, RMSE jumps far above MAE, flagging outliers. For items with zero sales in some weeks, MAPE cannot be computed.

As a manager, I use accuracy measures to choose between forecasting methods and to decide how much buffer stock to hold. The choice of measure should match the cost of errors. MAE is simple and treats all errors equally, in units we understand. When large errors are very costly, such as stock-outs of critical items, RMSE or MSE is better because squaring punishes big misses. MAPE is a percentage, so it is good for comparing accuracy across products or regions of different scale, but it is unreliable for low-volume or zero-demand items and is asymmetric. These measures show accuracy, not bias, so I also check the mean error.
